Analytical Approach
Ind-Ra continues to consider ONGC’s strong legal, operational, and strategic linkages with the government of India (GoI),
which held a 58.89% stake in the company as of FYE26 (FYE25: 58.89%), while arriving at the ratings. Furthermore, the
agency, as per its Parent Subsidiary Rating Linkage Criteria, continues to fully consolidate the financials of ONGC’s direct
subsidiaries, ONGC Videsh Limited (OVL; debt rated at ‘IND AAA’/Stable; 100% shareholding), Mangalore Refining and
Petrochemicals Limited (MRPL (consolidated);  debt rated at ‘IND AAA’/Stable); 71.63%), and ONGC Petro additions
Limited (OPaL; ‘IND AAA’/Stable; 95.96%), to which ONGC has extended support in the form of corporate guarantees apart
from equity infusions. Furthermore, Ind-Ra continues to factor in the dividend income received from Hindustan Petroleum
Corporation Limited (HPCL;  debt rated at ‘IND AAA’/Stable  and other subsidiaries,  joint ventures (JVs),  and associates
while assessing ONGC.
Detailed Rationale of the Rating Action
The ratings reflect ONGC’s majority ownership and strategic importance to the GoI, as it plays a key role in the country’s
energy security. The ratings are also supported by the dominant market position of ONGC in the domestic crude oil and
natural gas production business, with large proven reserves, a globally competitive cost structure, stable performance of its
subsidiaries, and its healthy financial position.  The credit profile of the ONGC Group, at the consolidated level, is
robust.  Furthermore,  the  company’s  strong  financial flexibility arising from its moderate gearing, large liquid
investments, and high cash balance provides additional comfort.
However,  the  ratings are susceptible to the inherent risk related to the  exploration and production (E&P)  business,
regulatory risks, geopolitical risk for overseas operations, large capex requirements to replace reserves, and high
contingent liabilities.

Detailed Description of Key Rating Drivers
Strong Linkages with GoI: ONGC is India’s largest domestic crude oil and natural gas producer, with proven reserves of
793.3 million metric tonnes of oil equivalent (mmtoe) as of March 2026 (ONGC: 517.88mmtoe; OVL: 265.27mmtoe; JVs:
10.16mmtoe). ONGC and OVL aid the GoI’s objective of ensuring energy security. OVL acts as India’s upstream producer
in international markets and helps in maintaining diplomatic and strategic ties with different countries. Moreover, OVL’s
capex and investment decisions benefit from its diplomatic ties with the GoI and are guided and approved by the latter. 
ONGC operates blocks allocated to it on a nomination basis by the GoI along with the blocks awarded through the New
Exploration Licensing Policy and Hydrocarbon Exploration and Licensing Policy; the latter two were introduced in FY98 and
FY16, respectively, to attract private participation in upstream production. Ind-Ra believes that ONGC, by the virtue of it
being the largest domestic oil producer, will continue to be strategically important for the GoI. ONGC’s importance to the
GoI is further supported considering the significant taxes and dividends paid by it to the exchequer. Ind-Ra does not expect
the GoI’s shareholding in ONGC to reduce below 51%, given the overseas bonds raised by ONGC stipulate the GoI’s
minimum holding at 51%. ONGC also has one GoI-nominated director and six independent directors on its board. 
Strong  Operating Metrics:  ONGC’s consolidated oil and gas production declined to 49.15mmtoe in FY26 (oil –
26.41mmtoe; gas – 22.73mmtoe) (FY25: 50.321mmtoe (oil – 27.118mmtoe; gas – 23.2mmtoe)), largely led by a production
decline in JVs. At the standalone level, the oil and gas production was stable at 18.34mmtoe and 19.54mmtoe, respectively
(FY25: 18.56mmtoe and 19.65mmtoe). OVL’s production slightly decreased to 9.67mmtoe in FY26 (FY25: 10.279mmtoe),
largely due to a natural decline in matured fields.
At the standalone level, ONGC’s reserve replacement ratio (2P) was 1.17x in FY26, with a reserve accretion of
44.01mmtoe from operated domestic areas, reflecting a healthy replenishment of its hydrocarbon reserves and supporting
the long-term sustainability of its exploration and production operations. ONGC’s total domestic 2P reserves was
709.32mmtoe as of 1 April 2026, including its share in non-operated JVs.
ONGC’s standalone oil and gas production declined 3.4% yoy to 9.444mmtoe in 1QFY27 (1QFY26: 9.779mmtoe).
Moreover, the crude oil production declined 4.9% yoy to 4.452mmt, while the natural gas production moderated 1.9% yoy
to 4.756 billion cubic metres. The decline was primarily attributable to reservoir complexities in the KG-DWN-98/2 block,
delays in pipeline replacement activities in the Western Offshore, and temporary well closures during the commissioning of
major projects. While the production has broadly stabilised sequentially, the continued yoy decline highlights the challenges
in arresting natural depletion across mature fields. Going forward, the stabilisation and recovery of production will likely
depend on the timely commissioning and ramp-up of key projects, including the Daman Upside Development Project
(DUDP), along with the expanded technical service provider programme across Western Offshore and the development of
discovered small fields. ONGC’s ongoing Western Offshore investment programme exceeding INR400 billion is likely to
support production recovery, with benefits progressively materialising from FY28.
Healthy  Credit Metrics:  Ind-Ra expects ONGC’s credit metrics to remain strong over the medium term despite a
moderation in profitability in FY26. The decline in FY26 earnings was primarily driven by lower crude oil realisations, lower
production from OVL, higher operating expenditure, and elevated foreign exchange losses. In contrast, MRPL reported a
substantial improvement in its profitability, led by higher gross refining margins (GRMs) in FY26. OPAL also turned EBITDA
positive in FY26, largely driven by structural changes, including the de-notification of the Dahej SEZ in March 2025, which
eliminated customs duty on domestic sales, and the allocation of competitively priced domestic gas from ONGC’s new
wells, resulting in 100% domestic feedstock tie-up.
ONGC’s standalone EBITDA decreased to INR617.2 billion in FY26 (FY25: INR652.36 billion), given the low realisation of
crude prices, but it was offset by a higher gas price realisation. However, Ind-Ra expects the consolidated profitability to

increase in FY27, given the elevated crude prices and gross refining margins on petroleum products amid the West Asia
conflict. Moreover, the company is likely to realise higher gas prices due to the new gas pricing policy, wherein any gas
from a new well or a well where well intervention has been done will be priced at 12% of the crude basket, higher than the
current administered pricing mechanism gas rate of USD6.75/million British thermal units. Currently, the revenue
contribution from new wells is around 38%.
The gross debt  consolidated by Ind-Ra  increased to  INR1,174  billion at FYE26  (FYE25: INR1,160  billion),  while the
unencumbered cash and liquid balances were INR312  billion  (INR260  billion);  the debt  comprised  INR445  billion
(INR402 billion) in OVL, INR143 billion (INR128 billion) in MRPL, and INR249 billion (INR250 billion) in OPaL, apart from
the standalone debt at ONGC. The net leverage (net debt/EBITDA) was 1.2x in FY26 (FY25: 1.4x).
ONGC’s standalone gross debt (incl. lease liabilities)  decreased to INR336.5  billion in FY26  (FYE25:
INR379  billion),  comprising  INR28.1 billion (INR25.7  billion)  in long-term foreign currency bonds, INR10 billion
(INR15  billion)  in non-convertible debentures, INR40.2 billion (INR43.5 billion) in short-term debt, and INR258 billion
(INR294 billion) in lease liabilities. However, the company remained net debt (excluding lease) negative on a standalone
level at FYE26. 
High Capex Likely to  Continue:  ONGC’s  average  standalone  capex per  annum  was INR350  billion-400  billion over
the  past  two years. The  company incurred a capex of  about  INR358  billion in FY26, with  about  INR94 billion  on
development drilling, about INR72 billion on exploration drilling, about INR162 billion on capital projects, and the balance
on surveys, research and development, integration, and JVs. Ind-Ra expects this trend to continue in the medium term as
the company looks to increase its petchem capacity and expand its refinery and renewable energy portfolio, along with the
domestic upstream capex. Any significant spend on expansion activities is a key rating monitorable. 
Profitability Dependent on Crude and Natural Gas Prices: ONGC derives around 63% of its gross revenues from the
sale of crude oil (FY26: INR838 billion; FY25: INR895  billion) and natural gas (INR363 billion; INR338  billion) on a
standalone basis, which are dependent on the movement of international crude prices and domestic gas prices (as fixed by
the Petroleum Planning & Analysis Cell, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas), respectively. Due to continued oversupply
concerns and softer global demand growth, the crude oil prices moderated in FY26, with the Brent crude averaging around
USD69/barrel of oil (bbl) (FY25: USD76.9/bbl; FY24: USD80.8/bbl; FY23: USD91.9/bbl). However, the trend reversed in
1QFY27, when the company realised a crude price of USD99.45/bbl due to the West Asia conflict. For the rest of FY27,
Ind-Ra expects the crude price to remain at elevated levels. Furthermore, ONGC’s profitability also depend on policy-level
changes by the GoI, such as the Special Additional Excise Duty.
High Contingent Liabilities:  ONGC’s standalone total contingent liabilities were INR715.7 billion at FYE26 (FYE25:
INR652.2 billion), of which INR402.4 billion (INR376.6  billion) was for the company and the balance INR313.3 billion
(INR275.8 billion) for the joint operations. The bulk of the contingent liabilities in the joint operations is attributed to the
unresolved issues related to the cost recovery and profit sharing for the RJ-ON-90/1 block (FY26: INR20 billion; FY25:
INR20  billion). The demand raised by the Directorate General of Hydrocarbon for Panna Mukta Tapti fields  was
INR152 billion in FY26 (FY25: INR139 billion). Any crystallisation of any of these major contingent liabilities could result in
lower-than-Ind-Ra-expected cash flows and higher-than-Ind-Ra-expected leverage.
Liquidity
Superior: ONGC’s standalone liquidity is supported by the sanctioned fund-based working capital limits of INR135 billion;
the average quarterly utilisation of the same was low at around 18.2% for the four quarters ended June 2026 and is likely to
have remained at similar levels thereafter. The company, at the standalone level, also had investments as its shareholding
in other public sector undertakings (Indian Oil Corporation Limited  (‘IND AAA’/Stable)  and GAIL (India) Limited (‘IND
AAA’/Stable)) of INR316 billion at FYE26 (FYE25: INR315 billion), while the cash balances (including other bank balances)
were INR286 billion (INR154 billion). Additionally, the company has a commerical paper limit of INR100 billion and a strong
capability to raise funds at attractive interest rates from the domestic market.
The company’s operating cash flow generation was healthy at INR716 billion at FYE26 (FYE25: INR746 billion), resulting
from the  healthy revenue  generation of INR1,325  billion (INR1,378 billion) and the EBITDA  of  INR617  billion
(INR652 billion). Moreover, ONGC received a dividend income of INR48 billion in FY26 (FY25: INR34.6 billion), while its

dividend outgo was INR166.7 billion (INR169.8 billion).
ONGC plans  a capex of  around INR300  billion for FY27  for the exploration, development, and purchase of capital
assets. Ind-Ra believes the debt requirements and the overall consolidated leverage would increase if OVL pursues any
sizeable investment opportunity. ONGC, on the standalone basis, has a long-term repayment obligation of INR48.4 billion
in FY27 and NIL in FY28. Ind-Ra believes the debt maturities, on the consolidated basis, can be managed by the company,
given its strong cash flows and ability to raise funds easily from domestic and international capital and banking markets.
Rating Sensitivities
Positive: Not applicable
Negative: A weakening of the linkages with the GoI could result in a negative rating action.

About the Company
ONGC is India’s largest domestic oil and gas producer. It was set up in the form of oil and gas division, under the
Geological Survey of India, in 1955, which was later converted into an Oil and Natural Gas Directorate. The directorate was
converted into a commission and later to a corporation in 1994. ONGC had a proven reserve of 806.9mmtoe as of March
2023.

About India Ratings
India Ratings and Research (Ind-Ra) is India's SEBI registered credit rating agency committed to providing India's credit
markets accurate, timely and prospective credit opinions. Built on a foundation of independent thinking, rigorous analytics,
and an open and balanced approach towards credit research, Ind-Ra has grown rapidly during the past decade, gaining
significant market presence in India's fixed income market.                                                                                                       
        
Ind-Ra currently maintains coverage of corporate issuers, financial institutions (including banks and insurance companies),
finance companies, urban local bodies, and structured finance and project finance companies. 
Headquartered in Mumbai, Ind-Ra has seven branch offices located in Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Chennai, Gurugram,
Hyderabad, Kolkata and Pune. Ind-Ra is recognised by the Securities and Exchange Board of India and the Reserve Bank
of India.  
Ind-Ra is a 100% owned subsidiary of the Fitch Group.
